newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia boosts defence spending, funds still short.
newsitem.headline: Russia boosts defence spending, funds still short.

text.p: The Russian government will boost defence spending next year to fund military reforms, a senior minister was quoted as saying on Friday.

Deputy Prime Minister and Economy Minister Yakov Urinson said 94 trillion roubles ($16.3 billion) would be spent on the armed forces next year, up from 83 trillion in this year and 64 trillion in 1996.

This would be targeted on new, modern equipment, research and combat training aimed at turning Russia's vast and demoralised Cold-War era military into a battle-ready force, he said in comments published by Interfax news agency on Friday.
But analysts say much bigger sums are needed to begin to fulfil Yeltsin's wish to turn Russia's bedraggled conscript force into a professional army by the turn of the century.
One said that the armed forces were in such a state that the government's latest move looked more like crisis management than well-planned reform.
In a further sign of the challenges ahead, the chief of Russia's chemical and biological defence said it would take more than $5 billion just to destroy the chemical weapons stockpile.
"The 94 trillion budgeted for 1998 is a considerable increase which will allow us to find the means to carry out military reform," Interfax quoted Urinson as saying.

New Defence Minister Igor Sergeyev, whose predecessor was sacked for not tackling reforms, declared war on waste in the army earlier this week by committing himself to a long campaign to trim and modernise Moscow's largely obsolescent armed forces.
Sergeyev was due to address parliament on Friday, part of a drive by the government to try to win reluctant deputies from the communist-dominated lower house around to its reforms.

There are estimated to be around 1.8 million men in the army, navy and air force, but even generals concede they are not sure of the exact figure, making it hard to assess progress on previous plans to cut 200,000 men this year.

Defence Council Secretary Yuri Baturin says there are actually 2.5 million men under arms, including border guards, interior ministry troops, customs and emergencies officials. Trade unions say 600,000 civilians also work in the military.
Yeltsin said on Thursday the armed forces should be reduced to 1.2 million although he did not give a target date.

"We don't need an army like the one we knew in the Soviet Union," Yeltsin said. What need do we have for five million men? None. What we need is an army of 1.2 million men. That is all. We will do it," he told reporters.
More specifically, the heads of the air force and ground troops said this week their personnel would be cut by more than a third by 2001 and similar cuts would fall across the board.

First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, who has led a new reform drive since March, said on Thursday a major reform of arms trading would begin this year, helping the government to raise an extra trillion roubles to help cut troop numbers.
"This trillion is extremely necessary for paying wages, arrears for those who will be made redundant. We have to pay them all arrears and all necessary benefits," he said.

In a plea for more funds, Colonel-General Stanislav Petrov said on Friday Russia needed more than $5 billion just to destroy 40,000 tonnes of chemical weapons, and that last year only one percent of that sum was earmarked from the budget.
Pavel Felgenhauer, defence analyst for the Sevodnya newspaper, said the defence ministry's coffers were empty.
"It is crisis management because basically the defence ministry is bankrupt," he said by telephone.

What Chubais, who heads a committee in charge of financing the modernisation of the military, appeared to be doing was plugging the worst gaps to avoid a mutiny and reorganising things to allow for reforms in better times, Felgenhauer said.

"The potential disenchantment is very high. Some people are paid, some are not. The army is full of nasty feelings. I don't say a mutiny is imminent but it is a threat and if things deteriorate it will get worse."
